deep.reconstruction:
This page is a young Gauss's elementary notes, c. 1795.

(1) Fermat's little theorem by induction on b. The header literally reads 'b^{a-1}/a is always an integer when a is prime'. As written that is false; the intended statement must be (b^a - b)/a ∈ Z for prime a (equivalently (b^{a-1}-1)/a ∈ Z when a does not divide b). The method Gauss announces is to replace b by b+1 and show the statement holds for b+1 once it holds for b. Implicit step (mine): (b+1)^a - (b+1) = (b^a - b) + Σ_{k=1}^{a-1} C(a,k) b^k. Each C(a,k) with 0<k<a is divisible by the prime a. So a | b^a - b implies a | (b+1)^a - (b+1). The base case is b=1 (or b=0). This is the classical binomial-induction proof.

(2) Which primes divide numbers a^2+1? Gauss poses the problem empirically. Primes dividing some a^2+1: 2, 5, 13, 17, 29, 37, 41, … Primes that never do: 3, 7, 11, 19, 23, 31, 43, … He says the underlying law is to be determined.

(3) A cancelled conjecture. If n, n' are consecutive primes of the first kind, then n' would be of the form n'k+n or nk+n'-n. The statement is ill-formed (n' cannot be of the form n'k+n) and is struck out.

(4) He remarks that it would be useful to extend such a table far, so the law might be found by induction. The table is: 2, 5, 13, 17, 29, 37, 41, 53, 61, 73, 89 (corrected from 83), 101, 97 (corrected from 103, written out of order), 109. This is exactly the set of primes ≤ 109 that equal 2 or are ≡ 1 mod 4.

(5) The same primes divide numbers a^2+4, and the others do not. In modern terms, for odd p, -4 = -1·2^2 is a quadratic residue iff -1 is. For p = 2, take a even.

(6) The inductive law. The first class consists of all primes 4n+1, the second of primes 4n-1. Hence every number a^2+1 has, apart from 2, only divisors of the form 4n+1. (Since a^2+1 ≢ 0 mod 4, 2 occurs at most once. Products of 4n+1 numbers are again 4n+1, so the claim holds for all odd divisors.)

The proof of the law is not given here. The next page begins a descent-type argument on l^2+m^2.
errors: The header as literally written ('b^{a-1}/a is an integer') is false; the intended statement must be (b^a - b)/a or (b^{a-1}-1)/a with a not dividing b. The induction b -> b+1 fits the form b^a - b.
The crossed-out conjecture about consecutive primes n, n' is ill-formed or false; Gauss rightly cancelled it.
Table slips 83 (≡3 mod 4) and 103 (≡3 mod 4) were corrected by Gauss to 89 and 97; 97 is left out of numerical order.
The 4n+1 law is stated by induction from the table only; no proof appears on this page.

results.what: Proof that a | b^a - b for prime a by induction on b using the binomial theorem
results.usually_credited_to: Fermat (statement 1640); proof by Leibniz (unpublished) and Euler (1736)

results.what: Odd primes dividing some a^2+1 are exactly those ≡1 mod 4; so a^2+1 has, besides 2, only divisors 4n+1
Primes dividing some a^2+4 are the same as those dividing some a^2+1

deep.surprise_reason: These are Gauss's early (c. 1795) inductive explorations of which primes have -1 as a quadratic residue, plus a standard proof of Fermat's little theorem. Gauss himself describes (Disquisitiones, art. 131 and elsewhere) rediscovering such results by induction in his youth. The content is classical (Fermat/Euler), and his early empirical work on it is known.

checkable.sympy: all(sympy.expand((b+1)**p-(b+1)-(b**p-b)-sum(sympy.binomial(p,k)*b**k for k in range(1,p))) == 0 for p in [2,3,5,7,11,13])
checkable.asserts: Binomial identity underlying the induction step (b symbol)

checkable.sympy: all(sympy.binomial(p,k)%p==0 for p in sympy.primerange(2,60) for k in range(1,p))
checkable.asserts: Middle binomial coefficients are divisible by a prime p

checkable.sympy: all(pow(b,p,p)==b%p for p in sympy.primerange(2,100) for b in range(0,50))
checkable.asserts: Fermat's little theorem b^p ≡ b mod p
Gauss's corrected table of primes dividing some a^2+1 up to 109

checkable.sympy: all(any((a*a+1)%p==0 for a in range(p)) == (p==2 or p%4==1) for p in sympy.primerange(2,2000))
checkable.asserts: p divides some a^2+1 iff p=2 or p≡1 mod 4

checkable.sympy: all(any((a*a+1)%p==0 for a in range(p)) == any((a*a+4)%p==0 for a in range(p)) for p in sympy.primerange(2,2000))
checkable.asserts: The same primes divide numbers a^2+1 and a^2+4

checkable.sympy: all(d%4==1 for a in range(1,300) for d in sympy.divisors(a*a+1) if d%2==1)
checkable.asserts: Every odd divisor of a^2+1 is ≡1 mod 4

transcription_corrections: Header formula: the intended statement must be (b^a - b)/a (or (b^{a-1}-1)/a); 'b^{a-1}/a' as transcribed is mathematically false.
Line 2: the struck-out text is 'Setzt man statt b b+1' and the interlinear insertion above it is 'bb' (uncertain); the sense is 'setting b+1 for b, one can show…'.
'können als Theiler v. Zahlen' is probably 'können Theiler von Zahlen dieser Form (aa+1) sein'.
In the table, '8[-3-]9' is 83 corrected to 89, and '[-103-] 97' is 103 corrected to 97.
